n: In this lecture we talk about cannabinoids, that is, cannabis and its narcological significance, and we also review the methods of its isolation and analysis. The outline is as follows: types of cannabis, phases of intoxication, toxicokinetics, colour reactions, paper and thin-layer chromatography, GLC and the pharmacological test. Key terms: cannabinoid, tetrahydrocannabinol, Pauli reagent, Fast Blue B, Duquenois reagent, Bouquet reagent and the “witness” solution.

First, let us get acquainted with cannabis itself. It is known as hashish, marijuana, plan, bang, dur, resin and other names. It is a mixture of resin, leaves and other parts obtained from cannabis flowers. More precisely, cannabis consists of the resin secreted from the flowers of Indian hemp, Cannabis sativa, and its active narcotic substance is tetrahydrocannabinol. Under the UN convention, any preparation containing cannabis is regarded as a narcotic drug, and its circulation is prohibited.

t: Study of cannabis and analytical questions
n: Cannabis was studied in 1966-1968: in those years its main constituents were separated by chromatography and the pharmacological effect was tested on laboratory animals. When analysing physical evidence, three questions are addressed. The first: what the product consists of and whether it contains parts of the cannabis plant. The second: whether it has a narcotic effect. The third: whether the product under examination has a common origin with a reliable cannabis sample.

Now, marijuana. Marijuana consists of the leaves, flowers and fruits from the upper part of the plant. The content of biologically active substances, that is, tetrahydrocannabinoids, in it is 13-15%. In dried marijuana about 400 chemical compounds and more than 70 cannabinoids have been identified. During smoking, the number of chemical substances in the smoke may reach 2000. As you can see, this is a very complex mixture.

Hashish may be liquid, waxy, greenish or dark. Hashish oil, in turn, is a thick extract or waxy liquid. On prolonged storage its colour and physical state change, so it is advisable to keep it in ethyl alcohol or sesame oil. Compare the content of the active substance: in marijuana 13-15%, in hashish 2-10%, and in hashish oil 10-60%. Therefore, the largest amount of active substance can be present in hashish oil.

t: Legal status and routes of use
n: Let us turn to the legal status. In 1942 in the USA the medical use of preparations derived from cannabis was permitted, and by 1992 marijuana had been placed on the list of controlled substances. This drug is included in the list of narcotic drugs of the Republic of Uzbekistan, and its use is prohibited. Cannabis is mainly smoked: 500-750 mg mixed with tobacco, or hashish oil added to tobacco. Oral use by chewing, infusions and addition to food also occur, while injection is rare.

The dependence, that is, the disease arising from the use of various cannabis products, is called cannabism. This group includes marijuana, hashish, bang, kif, hushush, plan, haras, dagga and others. The plant occurs in Asia, Africa and South America. When taken orally, the effect begins after 15-30 minutes. Remember: among narcotic drugs, cannabism ranks first.

We consider cannabis intoxication starting from the first use. When smoked for the first time, a pleasant feeling appears first, followed by nausea, a burning sensation in the mouth, salivation and dizziness. Then thirst, hunger, inflammation of the mucous membranes, a sensation of heat in the body and weightlessness develop. In addition, frequent laughter, distractibility of attention, acceleration of the pace of thought and tightness of speech appear.

The first phase is called the excitation stage. The user loses contact with those around, and irritable, hostile behaviour appears. The emotional state changes sharply: at times anger, at times an elevated mood up to the point of exaltation. There are continuous fantasies and illusions, the surroundings look multicoloured, and loud sounds and “echoes” are heard.

The second phase is the depression stage. Usually the transition from the first stage to the second is rapid. Colours fade, illusions disappear, fantasies die away and thinking is sharply inhibited. In their place come fear, fragmentary delusional ideas of persecution, the mood deteriorates sharply and autonomic crises occur. In other words, if excitation predominates in the first phase, depression predominates in the second.

t: Severity of intoxication and chronic effect
n: Symptoms depend on the dose taken, the rate of intake and the characteristics of the person’s higher nervous activity. Acute intoxication lasts 1-3 hours and ends in deep sleep, weakness and indifference. With heavier abuse, psychosis develops: hallucinations, persecutory ideas, delusions and marked motor agitation are observed. With regular use, after 2-6 months psychic asthenia, memory decline and apathy appear.

To believe that cannabis poisoning does not occur is wrong and dangerous. Cannabis acts strongly on the human higher nervous system, as a result leads to nervous disorders and does great harm to the growth of the body. Smoking cannabis together with opium, or using it with alcoholic drinks, leads to delirium and psychic changes.

Now the toxicokinetics of cannabinoids, according to the data in the textbook. Absorption begins within a few minutes of smoking. At 5-30 minutes cannabinoids and 9-THC reach high values, then fall rapidly in the blood. When taken by other routes, the duration of action is 1.5-3 hours. Cannabinoids are metabolised mainly in the liver, and within five days 80-90% of the dose is eliminated from the body.

t: Metabolism and excretion of THC (malaka No. 107)
n: THC undergoes extensive metabolism. Less than 1% is excreted unchanged in urine; mainly 25% is excreted in urine and 65% in faeces. With smoking, first-pass metabolism begins in the lungs, and with oral intake, in the liver. After 72 hours approximately 50% of the smoked THC is excreted as metabolites. The plasma half-life of THC is long, usually more than 20 hours.

The main excreted metabolite is 9-carboxy-THC, and its excretion is prolonged. In an occasional user the metabolite is detected in urine for 1-3 days. In a chronic smoker it is detected for more than a week after the last use. According to CDRH 1997 data, cannabinoids appear in urine 1-3 hours after intake and are detected for 1-7 days.

Let us review the screening and confirmation cut-offs. For marijuana in urine screening the cut-off is 100, and values of 50 and 20 ng/ml are also given. For confirmation, 15 ng/ml is used; this is the cut-off for 11-nor-9-carboxy-THC, that is, the main metabolite of THC. Remember: for screening there are several values, and for confirmation just one.

We now turn to the chemical composition of cannabis. Cannabis is a complex multicomponent mixture consisting of cannabinols, that is, dibenzopyran derivatives containing phenolic functional groups. The constantly occurring cannabinols are cannabinol, cannabidiol and tetrahydrocannabinol. Of these, only tetrahydrocannabinol has a narcotic effect. Therefore the narcotic property of cannabis is established by detecting THC.

The general scheme of analysis is carried out step by step. The physical evidence is first examined morphologically, and then chemical reactions are performed. The Pauli, Fast Blue B, Duquenois and Bouquet reactions are not specific for cannabis, so when they are positive, chromatography is necessary. Paper, thin-layer and gas-liquid chromatography are used to detect THC. If necessary, a pharmacological test is also performed.

Let us compare the colour reactions. Pauli reagent and Fast Blue B give a red-pink colour, then bluish, finally turning dark pink. With Duquenois reagent, pink, blue and then dark pink are formed. Bouquet reagent gives a red-brown colour. The sensitivity of all three reactions is 1 µg.

Isolation of cannabinoids is carried out by a simple method. To 1 g of the sample under examination, 10 ml of 96% alcohol is added and mixed well. After soaking for 1 hour, the mixture is filtered and checked for cannabinoids. The alcoholic extract is applied as a spot onto filter paper, dried, and sprayed with the reagents.

t: Pauli reagent and Fast Blue B
n: Pauli reagent is a mixture of 0.05% diazotised sulfanilic acid in a 10% solution of sodium carbonate. Fast Blue B is a 0.05% solution prepared in a 10% solution of sodium carbonate or in 1 M sodium hydroxide solution. If cannabinoids are present, a red-pink colour forms first, then bluish, and finally dark pink. The sensitivity of the reaction is 1 µg.

The Duquenois reaction. To prepare the reagent, 2 g of vanillin is dissolved in 100 ml of a 1% alcoholic solution of acetaldehyde. Then 2 ml of the reagent is added to 0.2 g of the sample and shaken for 1 minute, after which 1 ml of conc. HCl is added. Pink forms first, then blue, then dark pink. The sensitivity of the reaction is 1 µg.

The Bouquet reaction consists of several steps. Bouquet reagent is a mixture of 2 parts concentrated sulphuric acid and 3 parts 96% ethyl alcohol. 1 g of the sample is extracted three times with 5 ml of ethyl acetate each, the extract is cleaned with activated charcoal and evaporated. The residue is dissolved in 1 ml of acetone, and 0.5 ml of freshly prepared Bouquet reagent is added. As a result a red-brown colour forms; the sensitivity is 1 µg.

There is an important point in evaluating colour reactions. The above reactions are not specific for cannabis: cannabis plants not containing THC, and other cannabinoids, may also give them. If the results of the reactions are not positive, no further examination is needed, and the conclusion is given that the sample does not contain cannabis. With a positive result, paper, thin-layer and gas-liquid chromatographic analysis is performed to decide whether THC is present.

Preparation of the “witness” solution. Cannabinoids are difficult to isolate individually and are unstable, so a cannabis variety containing active THC is taken as the “witness”. 1 g of active cannabis is soaked in 10 ml of 96% ethyl alcohol for 24 hours at room temperature and filtered. The extract is made up to 10 ml with alcohol in a sealed brown container and stored in a refrigerator. It can be used for three months.

Paper chromatography. A strip of 3x30 cm is cut from chromatographic paper of the “S” grade. Mobile phase: freshly distilled dimethylformamide and cyclohexane in a 1:5 ratio, shaken in a separating funnel for 3 minutes. The lower layer is used to impregnate the paper, and the upper, cyclohexane layer is used as the mobile phase. The phase runs 250 mm, then the paper is dried at 60 °C.

The dried chromatogram is sprayed with Pauli reagent or Fast Blue B, and the substances are identified by Rf. The highest Rf is that of tetrahydrocannabinol, namely 0.83, and the lowest is that of cannabidiol, namely 0.21. Cannabinol is in the middle, 0.56. With Blue B, cannabidiol gives a yellowish-pink, cannabinol a red-pink, and tetrahydrocannabinol a violet colour.

We compare the Rf values by three methods. In paper chromatography, cannabidiol 0.21, cannabinol 0.56, THC 0.83, each with an accuracy of ±0.05. In thin-layer chromatography, Rf1 values are given for silicic acid and KSK plates. Here too the THC value is the highest: 0.98 on silicic acid and 0.91 on KSK. In all three methods THC has the highest Rf, and cannabidiol the lowest.

Thin-layer chromatography. Silica gel KSK and silicic acid plates are activated at 110 °C for 30 minutes. As the stationary phase, the plate is saturated with dimethylformamide; for this a vessel with dimethylformamide:benzene 1:1 is used. Then it is developed in a cyclohexane chamber to 15 cm. Because cannabinoids move slowly, the plate is chromatographed a second time in cyclohexane and designated Rf1.

To evaluate the thin-layer results, the plate is sprayed with Pauli reagent and Fast Blue B, and the colours are assessed. The Rf1 value of THC is 0.98±0.01 on silicic acid and 0.91±0.05 on KSK. In the table, cannabinol shows 0.75 on both plates, and cannabidiol 0.32 and 0.41. Cannabidiolic acid has the lowest values: 0.14 and 0.13.

Gas-liquid chromatography, that is, GLC conditions. The column is 2000x4 mm. The stationary phase is 3% methylsilicone elastomer SE-30, and the solid support is Chromosorb W,P or Sferochrom-1. The column temperature is 212 °C, and the vaporiser and detector temperature is 250 °C. The carrier gas is nitrogen or helium. The detector is a flame ionisation detector, and the analytical sample is 10 microlitres.

GLC is used to determine the composition and amount of cannabis cannabinoids. The content of active cannabinoids is determined on chromatographs with a programmable temperature regime, by the internal standard method. Cocaine hydrochloride is used as the internal standard.

Pharmacological examination. If chemical and physico-chemical methods are insufficient, additional pharmacological control may be carried out. It is performed by pharmacologist and toxicologist physicians. It is tested in cats or mice by the inhalation method: in a 70 l chamber a 2 g piece of cannabis is burned and the animals are kept for 30 minutes. Expected signs: short-term hyperactive excitation, mydriasis, salivation and immobility for up to 2 hours.

In evaluating the result, the main condition is this: without detecting THC or without pharmacological testing, the conclusion “cannabis” cannot be drawn. That is, colour reactions are performed first, then chromatography; if THC is detected or the pharmacological test confirms it, the conclusion is given as cannabis. Another important fact: traces of cannabis remain on the smoker’s oral cavity, lips, fingers and palm.

To establish that cannabis has been smoked, objects are collected. The hands of the suspected person are wiped with a cotton or gauze swab moistened with alcohol. From the saliva and oral cavity, a rinse is taken with 50 ml of 70% alcohol saturated with table salt. The swabs, saliva and rinse are sent to the toxicology laboratory in separate containers.

t: Isolation of cannabinoids from cotton and gauze
n: Isolation of cannabinoids from cotton and gauze. Pieces of cotton or gauze are extracted twice for 1 minute with 5 ml of diethyl ether. The ether is evaporated to 0.5-1 ml, and the colour reactions on filter paper are performed first. If the reactions are positive, THC is examined by thin-layer chromatography. If there is no coloured spot, there are no cannabinoids.

Analysis of saliva and rinse. From the suspected person, 10 ml of saliva and 50 ml of 70% alcoholic rinse saturated with table salt are combined and examined. 10 ml of the mixture is taken, mixed with 10 ml of saturated NaCl solution and extracted twice for 5 minutes with 5 ml of diethyl ether. The ether portions are combined, passed through 2 g of anhydrous Na2SO4, evaporated to 0.5 ml and examined by TLC. If THC is detected in the saliva and rinse, it can be concluded that the person has smoked cannabis.

Dose and intake. The minimum dose is 5 mg of THC. The effective dose by mouth is 50-200 mg, and by smoking 25-50 µg/kg. With smoking, the effect appears within a few minutes, and with oral intake within 20-120 minutes. The effect lasts 2-3 hours with smoking and 3-6 hours with oral intake.

Let us consider a practical case. As the object, an alcohol swab taken from the saliva and fingers of a person suspected of drug use is presented; for which substances analysis is needed. Outline of the solution: colour reactions for the swab, TLC for saliva and rinse; if THC is found, cannabis has been smoked. Review questions: what is cannabis; the formula of cannabinoids; establishing the fact of smoking; objects; chromatographic detection; products obtained from cannabis.
